requests.user:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws hold, with one exception: in the city of Ambry and the wards around it, a thing that is not written down stops being reliably itself. The effect is slow and dull rather than dramatic. An unrecorded corridor will, over a season, start to run a few feet short. An unregistered tool loses its temper and its edge. A person whose file is closed is not struck down; they are simply harder to remember, then harder to see, then gone from the accounts of everyone who knew them, until the only evidence they existed is what somebody wrote. Nothing about this is reversible by force. It is reversible by paperwork, which is why the Registry rules here.
technology: Roughly late nineteenth century, and skewed hard toward anything that copies or preserves. Ambry has pneumatic tube post between every ward office, carbon paper, wax cylinders, a functioning telegraph and no electricity in the residential wards. Presses, seals, indelible inks and lamp-lit copy rooms are the industry the city actually runs on. There are no engines to speak of outside the pumping stations, because an engine that is not maintained on a filed schedule stops working in ways engineers find distressing rather than interesting.
geographies: Ambry sits in a wide river delta that floods twice a year. The Registry occupies the whole of the high ground: eleven storeys of ward offices, copy rooms and stacks, built in rings around a courtyard nobody has permission to cross. Below it the Middle Wards spread out in numbered blocks, each one a warren of tenements and copying shops. Beyond the levee are the flood plains, unsurveyed and therefore unrecorded, where the Unwritten live in houses that move with the water. The Registry's own basements run four floors below the flood line and are dry, which nobody has ever satisfactorily explained.
races: Copyists' Line, Ledger-Kept, Marginalia, Unwritten
civilizations: One city, one institution, and a functional caste order underneath it. The Registry employs one adult in six and files the rest. Above the clerks sit the Inspectorate, who audit; above them the Sealed Room, which nobody in this story has seen. Below everyone are the Marginalia, whose records were damaged or amended and who consequently take the work that ought not be remembered. Out past the levee the Unwritten trade fish, salt and salvage into a city that will not put their names on a receipt. Everyone in Ambry is polite, and everyone counts the days since their file was last touched.


## Story Details
title: The Unrecorded Hour
genre: bureaucratic mystery
preface: The stamp is still in your hand and the ink is still wet, and there is an hour missing out of the middle of your own daybook. Not a blank line: a clean, ruled gap between four and five o'clock, in your handwriting, with the running total carried straight across it as though nothing needed to be entered at all. You have worked Ward Office 12 for eleven years and you have never carried a total across a gap in your life. Rain is coming off the levee and going sideways past the window. Somewhere down the long hallway a door closes, and then another, nearer -- the Inspectorate does its rounds at seven and it is twenty past six. Perrin's desk across the room has been cleared to the wood, and you cannot remember when, or by whom, or -- and this is the part that has your hands cold -- whether there was ever anybody sitting at it. There is one thing in this office nobody has audited in eleven years, and its door is behind you.
summary: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. Working out what happened in that hour means going through the Registry's own paperwork against it: the supply closet nobody has inventoried, the long hallway with the Inspectorate coming up it, and eventually the question of who has blank writs and why one was spent on a Marginalia clerk in Ward Office 12. The tone is dry, close and procedural, and the horror is entirely administrative.

name: The Long Hallway
teaser: Doors closing one after another, and shoes you can already hear.

## Instructions
Write this place out in full.
- The description is what the player reads on arrival. Address them as "you"
- Describe what is here now, not the history -- the history is the lore
- Stay consistent with the universe and with the teaser above
- Respect the stated length of each field

## What Is Lying Here
List AT MOST 3 portable things a player could pick up and carry away.
- Nothing is the right answer for most rooms. An empty list is a complete answer
- Only loose, portable things. Not the door, not the floor, not the machinery
  bolted to it -- something a person could put in a pocket or under an arm
- Each one must be consistent with the description you just wrote, and worth
  the player noticing
- Pick its use_kind from the supplied physical profiles. Ordinary is the
  default. Food and drink can be consumed without healing; healing is only
  a restorative dose this world permits. Firestarters burn combustible
  objects, levers pry jammed passages, lockpicks try locks, and a key only
  opens a passage explicitly matched to it. Mark combustible only when an
  ordinary firestarter can destroy the object. The engine owns the effects
  and their amounts; its description cannot grant extra powers
- If a thing has WRITING on it -- a note, a letter, a handbill, a label, a
  docket, a page, a sign -- mark it readable and WRITE OUT WHAT IS WRITTEN
  ON IT, exactly as it appears on the thing. The words themselves, not a
  description of them, and short enough to finish -- a few words, a line,
  or a few short lines. The game keeps those words and a player reading it
  twice reads the same ones
- Never name it after a person or after a place. Already spoken for in this story, so do not reuse: Odile Vance, Perrin Lasco, Halkett Rowe, filing press, ward stamp, Perrin's private index, copy-room apron, Ward Office 12 daybook

## Who Is Here
Write EXACTLY 3 people who are in this place right now.
- Anyone you write is somebody the player can walk up to and talk to, so they
  have to have a reason to be standing here and something they want
- Do not write the player, and do not write somebody passing through
- Never give them the name of a place, of a thing, or any name already
  spoken for above

Who they are is already decided. Write these people and do not change them:
  the 1st is Ledger-Kept, about 59, trans woman
  the 2nd is Marginalia, about 75, trans woman
  the 3rd is Copyists' Line, about 38, trans woman

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The 3 people who are in this place right now. Write all 3 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

  room's 4, not a target: fewer is a better answer than a door
  nobody needed
- Each exit is somewhere the player can reach directly from The Long Hallway
- One way out is a complete answer. A dead end, a cell, the bottom of a
  shaft: if the only way out is back the place the player came from, list
  that place and nothing else. Never invent a passage to reach a second
- When there is more than one, give the player a reason to prefer one
  over another
- Do not list The Long Hallway itself
- Say which of them have an INSIDE, and say NO INSIDE for almost all of
  them. Saying anything else makes the game build a whole floor plan of
  rooms in that place and send the player walking through them, so it is
  only ever right for a BUILDING somebody goes in at a door -- an inn, a
  keep, a counting house, a warren. A road, a shore, a clearing, a bridge,

  anybody there: a cellar, a back stair, a stretch of road, a room that is
  locked, a place the story has already emptied. Neither answer is the
  safe one

distance.description: How far it is. Pick the closest of these; the exact wording does not matter.

detail.description: You stand in a hallway of polished oak and brass fittings, its length stretching into dim lamplight that barely reaches the far doors. The air smells of beeswax and old paper, with a faint metallic tang from the radiators lining the walls. A series of identical doors, each marked with a small brass plaque, line both sides, and the sound of a door closing echoes from the far end, followed by the sharp, rhythmic click of approaching footsteps. The floorboards creak underfoot, and the faintest draft carries the scent of rain from the distant levee-side windows.
detail.lore: The Long Hallway connects the ward offices of the Registry’s Middle Wards, built to ensure clerks could move between departments without stepping into the unrecorded streets below. It was constructed in the early days of the Registry’s expansion, its design prioritizing symmetry and order over comfort. The brass plaques on each door are stamped with office numbers and dates of last audit, a reminder that even hallways must be accounted for. Over the years, the hallway has become a liminal space where clerks pass in silence, aware that the Inspectorate’s rounds are as inevitable as the tide.

people.appearance: A tall, silver-haired woman in a high-collared dress of deep navy, her posture rigid as though bracing against an unseen weight. Her hands, clasped behind her back, are ink-stained at the fingertips, and her spectacles catch the lamplight as she scans the hallway.
people.personality: Precise and methodical, she speaks in measured tones and expects the same from others. She treats strangers with polite detachment, though her eyes linger on anything out of place.
people.backstory: Elspeth Vey has served as a senior clerk in Ward Office 8 for thirty-two years, her file updated without fail every quarter. She is here now because she heard the doors closing and knows the Inspectorate’s schedule by heart; she intends to ensure no one lingers where they shouldn’t. She is quietly terrified of the idea that something—or someone—might have been erased without her noticing.

people.appearance: A slight, hunched woman with a face lined like old parchment, her gray hair tied back in a loose bun. She wears a patched coat over a dress that has seen better decades, and her fingers are gnarled from years of handling paper that was never meant to be read.
people.personality: She moves slowly but deliberately, her voice a rasping whisper. She is kind to those who acknowledge her, though she assumes they won’t remember her for long.
people.backstory: Mira Tallow was once a clerk in Ward Office 3, but her file was damaged in a fire and never fully restored. Now she drifts the Registry’s edges, collecting scraps of paper and discarded seals, hoping to piece together something that might resemble a name. She is here because she heard the footsteps and knows the Inspectorate does not look kindly on the Marginalia.

people.appearance: A broad-shouldered woman with auburn hair pinned severely back, her sleeves rolled to the elbows to reveal forearms dusted with chalk. She carries a ledger under one arm and a pencil tucked behind her ear, her expression one of mild irritation, as if the hallway itself has inconvenienced her.
people.personality: Direct and no-nonsense, she speaks in clipped sentences and has little patience for hesitation. She treats strangers with brisk efficiency, assuming they are either in her way or there to help.
people.backstory: Liora Dain is a copyist from Ward Office 17, sent to deliver a corrected manifest to Ward Office 12. She is running late, the ink on her ledger still damp, and the sound of the Inspectorate’s approach has her calculating how much trouble she’ll be in if she’s caught loitering. She doesn’t like being in the hallway any longer than necessary.
people.fears: audits, losing her place in the ledger

exits.name: Ward Office 12
exits.teaser: The door you came through, its brass plaque gleaming under the lamplight, and the damp scent of rain still clinging to the air beyond.

exits.name: Stairwell
exits.teaser: A narrow flight of stairs leading downward, its steps worn smooth by decades of hurried clerks.

exits.name: Ward Office 8
exits.teaser: A door marked with a brass 8, its hinges silent as the grave, and the faint sound of a quill scratching behind it.

items.description: A small, tarnished key with a simple bow, left on the windowsill of a transom above eye level. It looks like it might fit one of the hallway’s many doors.

people.appearance: A tall, silver-haired woman in a patched but immaculate clerk’s coat, her posture rigid as if bracing against an unseen weight. Her hands are ink-stained, and her face bears the faint lines of someone who has spent decades being overlooked.
people.personality: Quiet and precise, she speaks in measured tones, as if every word must be accounted for. She treats strangers with cautious politeness, but her eyes flicker toward exits, as if expecting to be asked to leave.
people.backstory: Mira Veyne was once a ledger clerk in Ward Office 7, but a misfiled amendment to her record relegated her to the Marginalia. She now works as a courier, delivering documents between wards, though she is rarely acknowledged. She is here because she was ordered to wait for an Inspector who has not yet arrived.
people.dislikes: unanswered questions, damp paper, being forgotten

people.appearance: A young woman with sharp features and a neat bun, her clerk’s apron crisp and her sleeves rolled to the elbow. She carries a stack of fresh daybooks under one arm, and her expression is one of barely contained impatience.
people.personality: Brisk and efficient, she speaks quickly, as if every second counts. She is polite but distracted, her attention already on the next task.
people.backstory: Lina Torve is a junior clerk in Ward Office 14, tasked with distributing new daybooks to the wards. She is here because she was told to deliver a set to Office 12, but she cannot find the right door and is growing frustrated.

people.appearance: A broad-shouldered person in their late forties, their clerk’s coat worn at the elbows and their hair tied back in a loose knot. They carry a battered ledger under one arm and a half-empty inkwell in the other, their expression weary but alert.
people.personality: Dry and no-nonsense, they speak with the authority of someone who has seen too much to be surprised. They treat strangers with a mix of curiosity and suspicion, as if weighing whether they are worth remembering.
people.backstory: Ren Solveig is a senior clerk in Ward Office 9, responsible for cross-referencing the day’s entries against the master ledger. They are here because they noticed a discrepancy in the records and are tracking it down before the Inspectorate does.
people.dislikes: careless errors, unmarked doors, the smell of wet paper

exits.name: Ward Office 12
exits.teaser: The door you came through, its brass plaque gleaming under the lamplight, and the faint scent of wet paper lingering in the air.

exits.name: Supply Closet
exits.teaser: A narrow door at the end of the hall, its paint chipped and its lock slightly rusted, as if rarely used.

exits.name: Inspectorate Stairwell
exits.teaser: A heavy oak door at the far end, its brass handle polished to a mirror shine, where the sound of approaching footsteps grows louder.

prompts.detail:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws hold, with one exception: in the city of Ambry and the wards around it, a thing that is not written down stops being reliably itself. The effect is slow and dull rather than dramatic. An unrecorded corridor will, over a season, start to run a few feet short. An unregistered tool loses its temper and its edge. A person whose file is closed is not struck down; they are simply harder to remember, then harder to see, then gone from the accounts of everyone who knew them, until the only evidence they existed is what somebody wrote. Nothing about this is reversible by force. It is reversible by paperwork, which is why the Registry rules here.
technology: Roughly late nineteenth century, and skewed hard toward anything that copies or preserves. Ambry has pneumatic tube post between every ward office, carbon paper, wax cylinders, a functioning telegraph and no electricity in the residential wards. Presses, seals, indelible inks and lamp-lit copy rooms are the industry the city actually runs on. There are no engines to speak of outside the pumping stations, because an engine that is not maintained on a filed schedule stops working in ways engineers find distressing rather than interesting.
geographies: Ambry sits in a wide river delta that floods twice a year. The Registry occupies the whole of the high ground: eleven storeys of ward offices, copy rooms and stacks, built in rings around a courtyard nobody has permission to cross. Below it the Middle Wards spread out in numbered blocks, each one a warren of tenements and copying shops. Beyond the levee are the flood plains, unsurveyed and therefore unrecorded, where the Unwritten live in houses that move with the water. The Registry's own basements run four floors below the flood line and are dry, which nobody has ever satisfactorily explained.
races: Copyists' Line, Ledger-Kept, Marginalia, Unwritten
civilizations: One city, one institution, and a functional caste order underneath it. The Registry employs one adult in six and files the rest. Above the clerks sit the Inspectorate, who audit; above them the Sealed Room, which nobody in this story has seen. Below everyone are the Marginalia, whose records were damaged or amended and who consequently take the work that ought not be remembered. Out past the levee the Unwritten trade fish, salt and salvage into a city that will not put their names on a receipt. Everyone in Ambry is polite, and everyone counts the days since their file was last touched.


## Story Details
title: The Unrecorded Hour
genre: bureaucratic mystery
preface: The stamp is still in your hand and the ink is still wet, and there is an hour missing out of the middle of your own daybook. Not a blank line: a clean, ruled gap between four and five o'clock, in your handwriting, with the running total carried straight across it as though nothing needed to be entered at all. You have worked Ward Office 12 for eleven years and you have never carried a total across a gap in your life. Rain is coming off the levee and going sideways past the window. Somewhere down the long hallway a door closes, and then another, nearer -- the Inspectorate does its rounds at seven and it is twenty past six. Perrin's desk across the room has been cleared to the wood, and you cannot remember when, or by whom, or -- and this is the part that has your hands cold -- whether there was ever anybody sitting at it. There is one thing in this office nobody has audited in eleven years, and its door is behind you.
summary: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. Working out what happened in that hour means going through the Registry's own paperwork against it: the supply closet nobody has inventoried, the long hallway with the Inspectorate coming up it, and eventually the question of who has blank writs and why one was spent on a Marginalia clerk in Ward Office 12. The tone is dry, close and procedural, and the horror is entirely administrative.


## The Place
name: The Long Hallway
teaser: Doors closing one after another, and shoes you can already hear.

## Instructions
Write this place out in full.
- The description is what the player reads on arrival. Address them as "you"
- Describe what is here now, not the history -- the history is the lore
- Stay consistent with the universe and with the teaser above
- Respect the stated length of each field

## What Is Lying Here
List AT MOST 3 portable things a player could pick up and carry away.
- Nothing is the right answer for most rooms. An empty list is a complete answer
- Only loose, portable things. Not the door, not the floor, not the machinery
  bolted to it -- something a person could put in a pocket or under an arm
- Each one must be consistent with the description you just wrote, and worth
  the player noticing
- Pick its use_kind from the supplied physical profiles. Ordinary is the
  default. Food and drink can be consumed without healing; healing is only
  a restorative dose this world permits. Firestarters burn combustible
  objects, levers pry jammed passages, lockpicks try locks, and a key only
  opens a passage explicitly matched to it. Mark combustible only when an
  ordinary firestarter can destroy the object. The engine owns the effects
  and their amounts; its description cannot grant extra powers
- If a thing has WRITING on it -- a note, a letter, a handbill, a label, a
  docket, a page, a sign -- mark it readable and WRITE OUT WHAT IS WRITTEN
  ON IT, exactly as it appears on the thing. The words themselves, not a
  description of them, and short enough to finish -- a few words, a line,
  or a few short lines. The game keeps those words and a player reading it
  twice reads the same ones
- Never name it after a person or after a place. Already spoken for in this story, so do not reuse: Odile Vance, Perrin Lasco, Halkett Rowe, filing press, ward stamp, Perrin's private index, copy-room apron, Ward Office 12 daybook

## Who Is Here
Write EXACTLY 3 people who are in this place right now.
- Anyone you write is somebody the player can walk up to and talk to, so they
  have to have a reason to be standing here and something they want
- Do not write the player, and do not write somebody passing through
- Never give them the name of a place, of a thing, or any name already
  spoken for above

Who they are is already decided. Write these people and do not change them:
  the 1st is Marginalia, about 58, trans woman
  the 2nd is Copyists' Line, about 20, female
  the 3rd is Copyists' Line, about 47, non-binary

## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws hold, with one exception: in the city of Ambry and the wards around it, a thing that is not written down stops being reliably itself. The effect is slow and dull rather than dramatic. An unrecorded corridor will, over a season, start to run a few feet short. An unregistered tool loses its temper and its edge. A person whose file is closed is not struck down; they are simply harder to remember, then harder to see, then gone from the accounts of everyone who knew them, until the only evidence they existed is what somebody wrote. Nothing about this is reversible by force. It is reversible by paperwork, which is why the Registry rules here.
technology: Roughly late nineteenth century, and skewed hard toward anything that copies or preserves. Ambry has pneumatic tube post between every ward office, carbon paper, wax cylinders, a functioning telegraph and no electricity in the residential wards. Presses, seals, indelible inks and lamp-lit copy rooms are the industry the city actually runs on. There are no engines to speak of outside the pumping stations, because an engine that is not maintained on a filed schedule stops working in ways engineers find distressing rather than interesting.
geographies: Ambry sits in a wide river delta that floods twice a year. The Registry occupies the whole of the high ground: eleven storeys of ward offices, copy rooms and stacks, built in rings around a courtyard nobody has permission to cross. Below it the Middle Wards spread out in numbered blocks, each one a warren of tenements and copying shops. Beyond the levee are the flood plains, unsurveyed and therefore unrecorded, where the Unwritten live in houses that move with the water. The Registry's own basements run four floors below the flood line and are dry, which nobody has ever satisfactorily explained.
races: Copyists' Line, Ledger-Kept, Marginalia, Unwritten
civilizations: One city, one institution, and a functional caste order underneath it. The Registry employs one adult in six and files the rest. Above the clerks sit the Inspectorate, who audit; above them the Sealed Room, which nobody in this story has seen. Below everyone are the Marginalia, whose records were damaged or amended and who consequently take the work that ought not be remembered. Out past the levee the Unwritten trade fish, salt and salvage into a city that will not put their names on a receipt. Everyone in Ambry is polite, and everyone counts the days since their file was last touched.


## Story Details
title: The Unrecorded Hour
genre: bureaucratic mystery
preface: The stamp is still in your hand and the ink is still wet, and there is an hour missing out of the middle of your own daybook. Not a blank line: a clean, ruled gap between four and five o'clock, in your handwriting, with the running total carried straight across it as though nothing needed to be entered at all. You have worked Ward Office 12 for eleven years and you have never carried a total across a gap in your life. Rain is coming off the levee and going sideways past the window. Somewhere down the long hallway a door closes, and then another, nearer -- the Inspectorate does its rounds at seven and it is twenty past six. Perrin's desk across the room has been cleared to the wood, and you cannot remember when, or by whom, or -- and this is the part that has your hands cold -- whether there was ever anybody sitting at it. There is one thing in this office nobody has audited in eleven years, and its door is behind you.
summary: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. detail.description: You stand in the belly of the *Vestry*, where the hull’s ribs press close and the air smells of tar and old paper. A single oil lamp swings from a beam, casting long shadows over stacks of yellowed dockets and ledgers bound in salt-stiffened leather. The deck above creaks with the shift of the tide, and the damp wood groans as if remembering the sea. A narrow companionway leads up to the courtroom, its steps worn smooth by generations of boots. The light is dim, but enough to read by if you hold the page close.
detail.lore: The *Vestry* was a revenue cutter that ran aground on Gallows Rock in 1836 and was never refloated. Over time, the court repurposed her as its archive, storing records, oaths, and verdicts in her hold. The ship’s timbers have long since settled into the rock, and now she serves as both vestry and symbol: the law’s memory, preserved by the same water that once threatened to claim her. The Justicars and Bell-Keepers treat her as sacred ground, though the Shorefolk sometimes joke she’s the only vessel on the coast that’s never moved under her own power.

people.personality: Sharp-tongued but fair, she speaks with the confidence of someone who knows the tides better than most. She treats strangers with cautious curiosity, as if sizing them up for a trade.

She came to the *Vestry* this morning to retrieve a ledger she’d borrowed for a dispute over a sunken cargo, but found the door locked and has been waiting for someone with a key. She’s not happy about the delay.

people.fears: being trapped below water, the dark

people.personality: Quiet and deliberate, he speaks in measured tones, as if every word must be weighed before it’s given. He regards strangers with a mixture of suspicion and quiet respect.
people.backstory: Eldrin Moss is a retired grazier and one of the few Marshborn who still remember the *Vestry*’s arrival. He’s here to consult the old tide records, convinced the current Bell-Keeper has made a mistake in the chalk. He’s been waiting for the Justicar to finish his business so he can speak to him.

people.appearance: A Marshborn man with a hunched back and a permanent squint, as if the light always bothers him. His fingers are stained with ink, and he carries a satchel slung over one shoulder.
people.personality: Muttering and distracted, he talks more to himself than to others, though he’ll answer a direct question with surprising clarity. He’s forgetful but not unkind.
people.backstory: Tobin Reed is the court’s scribe, tasked with transcribing the day’s proceedings. He’s here early to retrieve a fresh ledger from the *Vestry*’s stores, but he’s become sidetracked by an old case file he can’t resist reading. He doesn’t notice the time slipping.

prompts.detail:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws, with one local exception the courts are built around: on this coast an oath spoken over standing salt water binds, and an oath spoken over dry ground does not. Nobody has explained it and everybody has arranged their life around it. A sworn statement made on the causeway at low water holds a man in place -- he cannot walk away from it, cannot contradict it, and will find his own mouth refusing the lie. The same words spoken inland are only words. The binding lasts exactly as long as the water that heard it stays where it is, which on this coast is about six hours.
technology: Sail, tar, oil lamp and iron. Roughly eighteenth century and skewed entirely toward the sea: block and tackle, chain, dredging gear, tide tables computed by hand and reprinted every spring. There is no telegraph and no engine on the coast. The most advanced instrument in the county is the Assize bell, cast to a pitch that carries over surf, and the second is the tide-slate, a ruled board of black slate on which the day's high water is chalked and which no one is permitted to erase but the Bell-Keeper.
geographies: A drowned coast of mud flats, salt marsh and islands that are only islands twice a day. The Assize causeway runs a mile out from the shore to Gallows Rock and is walkable for about five hours either side of low water. On the rock stand the court, the tide post and the beached hulk of the *Vestry*, a revenue cutter that came ashore ninety years ago and was never floated off. Inland the marsh runs to grazing, and beyond that the county town, which the Assizes visit once and never twice.
races: Bell-Keepers, Circuit Justicars, Marshborn, Shorefolk
civilizations: One county, one court, and a hard division between the people of the shore and the people of the marsh. The shore lives by salvage, oysters and the wrecking trade and considers the law a weather event. The marsh lives by grazing and considers itself the county's conscience. Above both sit the Justicars, appointed for life and travelling in circuit, and beside them the Bell-Keepers -- a guild of one family per coast, who read the water and are the only people whose word can rise a court. Everyone here can tell you how long they have until the water turns.


## Story Details
title: The Salt Assizes
genre: tidal legal mystery
preface: You have rung this court up and down for nineteen years and you have never once been wrong about the water, which is why the chalk on the tide-slate is wrong in somebody else's hand. High water is written as ten minutes past eight. High water is at seven. You wrote seven yourself, last night, on a dry board in a still room, and the figure on the slate now is not yours and is close enough to yours to pass. Out at the post, Neb Halloran has been chained since the ebb for a wrecking nobody on this coast believes he did alone, and his hearing is set for the last hour before the turn -- an hour that, on that chalk, does not exist. The Justicar is already in the court with his gown on. The bell is on its hook. Whoever moved seventy minutes has given the water time to do what the court would have had to sign for.
summary: The player is Coraith Vell, Bell-Keeper of the Assize causeway, who finds the day's high water altered by seventy minutes in a hand that is almost her own. The chained man at the tide post has a hearing in an hour the false chalk has erased, so working out who changed it means reading the court's own papers against the water: the Justicar who needs a verdict, the wreck that serves as the vestry, and the question of who benefits from a drowning the record will call a delay. The tone is cold, procedural and out of doors, and the clock is the sea.

history.content:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws, with one local exception the courts are built around: on this coast an oath spoken over standing salt water binds, and an oath spoken over dry ground does not. Nobody has explained it and everybody has arranged their life around it. A sworn statement made on the causeway at low water holds a man in place -- he cannot walk away from it, cannot contradict it, and will find his own mouth refusing the lie. The same words spoken inland are only words. The binding lasts exactly as long as the water that heard it stays where it is, which on this coast is about six hours.
technology: Sail, tar, oil lamp and iron. Roughly eighteenth century and skewed entirely toward the sea: block and tackle, chain, dredging gear, tide tables computed by hand and reprinted every spring. There is no telegraph and no engine on the coast. The most advanced instrument in the county is the Assize bell, cast to a pitch that carries over surf, and the second is the tide-slate, a ruled board of black slate on which the day's high water is chalked and which no one is permitted to erase but the Bell-Keeper.
geographies: A drowned coast of mud flats, salt marsh and islands that are only islands twice a day. The Assize causeway runs a mile out from the shore to Gallows Rock and is walkable for about five hours either side of low water. On the rock stand the court, the tide post and the beached hulk of the *Vestry*, a revenue cutter that came ashore ninety years ago and was never floated off. Inland the marsh runs to grazing, and beyond that the county town, which the Assizes visit once and never twice.
races: Bell-Keepers, Circuit Justicars, Marshborn, Shorefolk
civilizations: One county, one court, and a hard division between the people of the shore and the people of the marsh. The shore lives by salvage, oysters and the wrecking trade and considers the law a weather event. The marsh lives by grazing and considers itself the county's conscience. Above both sit the Justicars, appointed for life and travelling in circuit, and beside them the Bell-Keepers -- a guild of one family per coast, who read the water and are the only people whose word can rise a court. Everyone here can tell you how long they have until the water turns.


## Story Details
title: The Salt Assizes
genre: tidal legal mystery
preface: You have rung this court up and down for nineteen years and you have never once been wrong about the water, which is why the chalk on the tide-slate is wrong in somebody else's hand. High water is written as ten minutes past eight. High water is at seven. You wrote seven yourself, last night, on a dry board in a still room, and the figure on the slate now is not yours and is close enough to yours to pass. Out at the post, Neb Halloran has been chained since the ebb for a wrecking nobody on this coast believes he did alone, and his hearing is set for the last hour before the turn -- an hour that, on that chalk, does not exist. The Justicar is already in the court with his gown on. The bell is on its hook. Whoever moved seventy minutes has given the water time to do what the court would have had to sign for.

The chained man at the tide post has a hearing in an hour the false chalk has erased, so working out who changed it means reading the court's own papers against the water: the Justicar who needs a verdict, the wreck that serves as the vestry, and the question of who benefits from a drowning the record will call a delay. The tone is cold, procedural and out of doors, and the clock is the sea.

## Universe Details
physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.


## Story Details
title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.

The game's tone is grounded, atmospheric, and focused on mystery and survival in a world that refuses to stay still.

history.content:
## Universe Details
physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.

title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.
summary: The player is a cartographer hired by the Lunar Sovereigns to map the nightly rearrangements of the city of Nocturnis, where buildings, streets, and landmarks shift with the moon's phases due to residual magical energy called Nocturna. detail.description: You stand inside the hollow base of the Bell of Saint Aravel, where the great bronze bell hangs suspended above you, its surface etched with silver runes that catch the dim moonlight filtering through narrow slits in the stone. The air hums with the faint resonance of the last chime, and the scent of aged metal and damp stone lingers. A spiral staircase winds upward along the inner wall, its iron steps worn smooth by centuries of use. The floor is littered with a few scattered tools and a single, half-burned candle stub, its wax pooled in a shallow depression in the stone.
detail.lore: The Bell of Saint Aravel was once part of a grand cathedral that stood in the heart of Nocturnis before the Great War. The cathedral was destroyed, but the bell tower remained, its foundation anchored deep into the bedrock, making it one of the few structures immune to Nocturna’s rearrangements. The bell itself is said to be enchanted, its chimes guiding lost travelers back to safety, though its magic has faded over time. Now, it serves as a landmark for those navigating the ever-shifting city.

people.appearance: A stout, elderly Crystal Dwarf with a thick, braided white beard that nearly reaches his waist. His leathery face is lined with deep wrinkles, and his hands, though gnarled with age, still grip a small hammer with practiced ease. He wears a heavy apron stained with soot and metal shavings.
people.personality: Gruff but not unkind, Thorgar speaks in a slow, deliberate manner, as if weighing each word before it leaves his mouth. He treats strangers with cautious respect, though his patience wears thin with foolishness.
people.backstory: Thorgar Ironvein was once a master smith in the Crystal Peaks, but after the Great War, he wandered into Nocturnis, drawn by the city’s strange magic. He now spends his days maintaining the few static structures like the Bell of Saint Aravel, believing that preserving these relics is a way to honor the past. He hopes to one day restore the bell’s enchantment.
people.likes: fine craftsmanship, quiet company, old stories
people.dislikes: wastefulness, loud noises, disrespect for history

people.appearance: A gaunt Nocturna-Blighted woman with hollow cheeks and eyes that seem to flicker with an unnatural glow. Her dark hair is streaked with silver, and her fingers twitch as if she’s constantly reaching for something just out of grasp. She wears a tattered cloak that seems to shift colors in the dim光.
people.personality: Lysara is restless and speaks in fragmented sentences, her mind often drifting mid-thought. She is wary of strangers but can be coaxed into conversation with patience, though her words are often cryptic or tinged with paranoia.
people.backstory: Lysara Veyne was once a scholar who studied Nocturna’s effects on the city, but prolonged exposure to the magic has left her mind fractured. She now wanders the static points of Nocturnis, convinced that the city’s rearrangements are a message she must decipher. She lingers near the Bell of Saint Aravel, believing its chimes hold clues to the city’s secrets.
people.dislikes: bright lights, sudden movements, being touched

prompts.detail:
## Universe Details
physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.


## Story Details
title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.
summary: The player is a cartographer hired by the Lunar Sovereigns to map the nightly rearrangements of the city of Nocturnis, where buildings, streets, and landmarks shift with the moon's phases due to residual magical energy called Nocturna. As they work, they uncover conspiracies within the Sovereigns, encounter the displaced peoples of the Scorch Nomads and Verdant Folk, and grapple with the disorienting effects of prolonged exposure to Nocturna, which causes memory loss. The game's tone is grounded, atmospheric, and focused on mystery and survival in a world that refuses to stay still.

## Universe Details
physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. These lines can be tapped by blood rituals, but each use drains the caster’s lifespan by exactly one day per minute of magic. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.

title: The Iron Gate Descends
genre: dark fantasy
preface: The iron gate groans as it settles into the stone, its teeth biting into the threshold with a finality that echoes through the cavern. You stand in the dim glow of bioluminescent fungi, the air thick with the scent of damp earth and old blood. Your gauntleted hand rests on the hilt of your Veldarian sword, its edge still sharp despite the weight of the blackened plate armor pressing into your shoulders. The prince’s signet ring, cold in your palm, was found in the mud outside this gate—proof he passed this way. Behind you, the tunnel slopes upward, but the way forward is a yawning maw of obsidian, the walls slick with moisture. Somewhere in the dark, something skitters.

The prince’s signet ring, discovered in the mud, confirms his passage into the tunnels. The air is thick with the scent of damp earth and the faint glow of fungi, while the distant sound of movement hints at unseen dangers ahead. The Church’s decree to retrieve the prince or die trying weighs heavily, but the immediate threat is the darkness itself.

history.content:
## Universe Details
physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. These lines can be tapped by blood rituals, but each use drains the caster’s lifespan by exactly one day per minute of magic. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.


## Story Details
title: The Iron Gate Descends
genre: dark fantasy
preface: The iron gate groans as it settles into the stone, its teeth biting into the threshold with a finality that echoes through the cavern. You stand in the dim glow of bioluminescent fungi, the air thick with the scent of damp earth and old blood. Your gauntleted hand rests on the hilt of your Veldarian sword, its edge still sharp despite the weight of the blackened plate armor pressing into your shoulders. The prince’s signet ring, cold in your palm, was found in the mud outside this gate—proof he passed this way. Behind you, the tunnel slopes upward, but the way forward is a yawning maw of obsidian, the walls slick with moisture. Somewhere in the dark, something skitters.
summary: A Durnish knight, clad in heavy blackened plate, stands at the threshold of the goblin caves beneath the Ashen Spire, having just forced open an iron gate. The prince’s signet ring, discovered in the mud, confirms his passage into the tunnels. The air is thick with the scent of damp earth and the faint glow of fungi, while the distant sound of movement hints at unseen dangers ahead. The Church’s decree to retrieve the prince or die trying weighs heavily, but the immediate threat is the darkness itself.

history.content:
## Universe Details
physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. These lines can be tapped by blood rituals, but each use drains the caster’s lifespan by exactly one day per minute of magic. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.


## Story Details
title: The Iron Gate Descends
genre: dark fantasy
preface: The iron gate groans as it settles into the stone, its teeth biting into the threshold with a finality that echoes through the cavern. You stand in the dim glow of bioluminescent fungi, the air thick with the scent of damp earth and old blood. Your gauntleted hand rests on the hilt of your Veldarian sword, its edge still sharp despite the weight of the blackened plate armor pressing into your shoulders. The prince’s signet ring, cold in your palm, was found in the mud outside this gate—proof he passed this way. Behind you, the tunnel slopes upward, but the way forward is a yawning maw of obsidian, the walls slick with moisture. Somewhere in the dark, something skitters.
summary: A Durnish knight, clad in heavy blackened plate, stands at the threshold of the goblin caves beneath the Ashen Spire, having just forced open an iron gate. The prince’s signet ring, discovered in the mud, confirms his passage into the tunnels. The air is thick with the scent of damp earth and the faint glow of fungi, while the distant sound of movement hints at unseen dangers ahead. The Church’s decree to retrieve the prince or die trying weighs heavily, but the immediate threat is the darkness itself.


## The Place
name: obsidian maw
teaser: The yawning black tunnel ahead, its walls slick with moisture and the distant sound of skittering claws echoing from the dark.

## Instructions
Write this place out in full.
- The description is what the player reads on arrival. Address them as "you"
- Describe what is here now, not the history -- the history is the lore
- Stay consistent with the universe and with the teaser above
- Respect the stated length of each field

## What Is Lying Here
List AT MOST 3 portable things a player could pick up and carry away.
- Nothing is the right answer for most rooms. An empty list is a complete answer
- Only loose, portable things. Not the door, not the floor, not the machinery
  bolted to it -- something a person could put in a pocket or under an arm
- Each one must be consistent with the description you just wrote, and worth
  the player noticing
- Pick its use_kind from the supplied physical profiles. Ordinary is the
  default. Food and drink can be consumed without healing; healing is only
  a restorative dose this world permits. Firestarters burn combustible
  objects, levers pry jammed passages, lockpicks try locks, and a key only
  opens a passage explicitly matched to it. Mark combustible only when an
  ordinary firestarter can destroy the object. The engine owns the effects
  and their amounts; its description cannot grant extra powers
- If a thing has WRITING on it -- a note, a letter, a handbill, a label, a
  docket, a page, a sign -- mark it readable and WRITE OUT WHAT IS WRITTEN
  ON IT, exactly as it appears on the thing. The words themselves, not a
  description of them, and short enough to finish -- a few words, a line,
  or a few short lines. The game keeps those words and a player reading it
  twice reads the same ones
- Never name it after a person or after a place. Already spoken for in this story, so do not reuse: Veythra the Silent, iron key, prince's signet ring

## Who Is Here
Write EXACTLY 1 person who is in this place right now.
- Anyone you write is somebody the player can walk up to and talk to, so they
  have to have a reason to be standing here and something they want
- Do not write the player, and do not write somebody passing through
- Never give them the name of a place, of a thing, or any name already
  spoken for above

Who they are is already decided. Write these people and do not change them:
  the 1st is Trollkin, about 51, trans man

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. people.description: The 2 people who are in this place right now. Write all 2 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

## Universe Details
physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. These lines can be tapped by blood rituals, but each use drains the caster’s lifespan by exactly one day per minute of magic. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.


## Story Details
title: The Iron Gate Descends
genre: dark fantasy
preface: The iron gate groans as it settles into the stone, its teeth biting into the threshold with a finality that echoes through the cavern. You stand in the dim glow of bioluminescent fungi, the air thick with the scent of damp earth and old blood. Your gauntleted hand rests on the hilt of your Veldarian sword, its edge still sharp despite the weight of the blackened plate armor pressing into your shoulders. The prince’s signet ring, cold in your palm, was found in the mud outside this gate—proof he passed this way. Behind you, the tunnel slopes upward, but the way forward is a yawning maw of obsidian, the walls slick with moisture. Somewhere in the dark, something skitters.
summary: A Durnish knight, clad in heavy blackened plate, stands at the threshold of the goblin caves beneath the Ashen Spire, having just forced open an iron gate. The prince’s signet ring, discovered in the mud, confirms his passage into the tunnels. The air is thick with the scent of damp earth and the faint glow of fungi, while the distant sound of movement hints at unseen dangers ahead. The Church’s decree to retrieve the prince or die trying weighs heavily, but the immediate threat is the darkness itself.

## Universe Details
physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. These lines can be tapped by blood rituals, but each use drains the caster’s lifespan by exactly one day per minute of magic. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.
